title: The good shepherd (John 10:1–18)
hook: he knows his sheep by name and they know his voice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the healed man stood his ground: one thing I know. Your line was now I see. What did you notice that you hadn't seen before? Day five hundred twelve.

In a crowded airport, a hundred voices blur into noise. Then someone, far off, says your name, and your head turns before you've decided anything. Your name cuts through. Travelers in the Middle East have described something like it with sheep: several flocks sheltering together overnight, all mixed up, and in the morning each shepherd simply calls, and his own sheep sort themselves out and follow him. The man born blind has just been thrown out of the synagogue. And Jesus, right after, starts talking about sheep, voices and names.
screen: `YOUR NAME IN A CROWDED AIRPORT.` → `MIXED FLOCKS, ONE CALL.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE BLIND MAN.`

segments.voice: Jesus sets the scene: a sheepfold, a wall, a gate, a keeper at the gate. A thief climbs over the wall. The shepherd comes in by the door, and the Douay-Rheims says: "the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Notice the order. Name first, then leading. He doesn't drive them from behind with a stick. He walks ahead and they follow a voice they know. Then comes another great I am. "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." He compares a hired hand, who sees the wolf coming and runs, because the sheep aren't his. The good shepherd stays, and more than stays. The word John uses for good, kalos, also carries the sense of beautiful, noble, the real thing. And then a line about outsiders: other sheep I have, that are not of this fold; them also I must bring. Whatever else that means, the flock is bigger than the people standing there. And look where John sets this speech. A man has just been pushed out of his community for telling the truth, and Jesus goes looking for him. The shepherd keeps the one who was thrown out. Christians loved this picture early. Some of the oldest Christian paintings, on the walls of the Roman catacombs, show a young shepherd with a lamb across his shoulders. In the Catholic calendar, the fourth Sunday of Easter is called Good Shepherd Sunday, and the Church prays that day for vocations, for people called to shepherd others.
screen: `THE FOLD, THE GATE, THE THIEF.` · `HE CALLS THEM BY NAME.` · `THE HIRED HAND RUNS; HE STAYS.` · `THE SHEPHERD ON THE CATACOMB WALL.` · then, large: `THE GOOD SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen. Sit comfortably and let the sounds around you come in: traffic, a fan, a bird, your own breath. Don't chase any of them. Then, under all the noise, imagine your own first name being said once, quietly, by someone who means you well. Let it land. If you pray, you can hold the line, he calleth his own sheep by name, and listen for his voice in the quiet. If you don't, just rest in the feeling of being known by name. The bell holds the time.
Kalos. The Greek word for good that also means noble, beautiful: what Jesus calls the shepherd who calls his own by name and lays down his life for them. Today's word.
Your line: he knows my name. Today, use someone's name when you thank them, the cashier, the driver, a coworker. Watch what it does. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, Catholics hear a reading from John 10 at Mass, and the Church prays that day for vocations to the priesthood and religious life.

fork.setup: you're a hired hand watching someone else's sheep, and a wolf comes over the hill. what does Jesus say a hired hand does?
fork.reveal: the hired hand runs, because the sheep aren't his. the good shepherd is the one who stays and gives his life.

original.note: Greek: the good shepherd (John 10:11). kalos also means noble, beautiful.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus holding a lamb.
what it means: a shepherd who knows each one by name, walks ahead, and stays when the wolf comes.
what a scholar hears: it follows straight on from John 9, where the healed man is cast out; the Good Shepherd image appears in Roman catacomb art.

notes: Mixed flocks sorting by the shepherd's call: framed as travelers' descriptions, not as a fact about all shepherding. Confirm the framing is acceptable.
Kalos as 'good, noble, beautiful': standard lexicon range. Confirm.
Good Shepherd images in the Roman catacombs (e.g. Callixtus, Priscilla) as among the earliest Christian paintings. Confirm.
Fourth Sunday of Easter as Good Shepherd Sunday and World Day of Prayer for Vocations. Confirm.
'Other sheep I have' (10:16) is quoted in paraphrase; its interpretation is left open on purpose.
Audit (second sample): the garbled sentence 'it fits where it falls' and the stock 'a line people tend to skip' reworded.
